text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPaleontologyCheck Out the Mouthparts on This New Prehistoric InsectBut it was strictly a vegetarianJCBy Jake Currie5:30 PM CDT on October 9, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleAnyone who’s seen Jurassic Park knows fossilized amber is lousy with trapped insects. While we can’t extract their juices to make dinosaurs, many of these insects are preserved in pristine detail and offer an invaluable record into what life was like tens and even hundreds of millions of years ago. Now, paleontologists have identified a new species of insect frozen in the ancient tree sap, and it’s got specialized mouthparts unlike any other insect living today.Powered By 10 ShareNextStayThis new prehistoric insect is a member of the order hemiptera (the true bugs) and the suborder auchenorrhyncha, which includes insects like cicadas, leafhoppers, and treehoppers. A team of paleontologists from Tel Aviv University identified the species from specimens trapped in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber, calling it Cretodorus noonoo or “Noo-Noo.” They recently published their description of the prehistoric insect (appropriately) in the journal Insects.Read more: “What Happened to the Ancient Bug Giants of 300 Million Years Ago?”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
